entities.summary:
Diogo de Silves, whose very identity remains shrouded in the mists of early 15th-century Atlantic exploration, is widely presumed to be the Portuguese navigator credited with the rediscovery or first documented European sighting of the western Azores islands in 1427. His alleged feat marks a pivotal, albeit sparsely recorded, moment in the Portuguese Age of Discovery, contributing to the gradual outward expansion of European maritime knowledge beyond continental coastlines and into the open ocean. While historical records offer tantalizing but incomplete glimpses into his life, his name is inextricably linked with the initial phase of permanent Portuguese settlement in the archipelago, laying groundwork for future transatlantic ventures.

The core event attributed to Diogo de Silves is the charting of the westernmost islands of the Azores, specifically Corvo and Flores, in 1427. This voyage, undertaken perhaps as part of a larger exploratory thrust sanctioned by Infante Henry the Navigator, extended the known limits of the European world, pushing beyond the previously sighted eastern and central groups of the archipelago. His expedition would have involved considerable navigational skill, relying on rudimentary instruments like the quadrant and astrolabe, alongside practical seamanship, to traverse hundreds of miles of uncharted Atlantic waters. The precise details of his route, the composition of his crew, and the vessel he commanded are, however, lost to history, existing primarily through later cartographic references and chronicles.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Diogo Silves's alleged rediscovery of the western Azores in 1427 expanded European knowledge of the Atlantic and directly led to the archipelago's strategic importance as a transatlantic hub for centuries. This event significantly advanced Portuguese maritime exploration and colonization efforts.
